content: Women diagnosed with ovarian cancer are at a significant risk of malnutrition, with reported incidence rates ranging from 28% to 67%. Nutritional interventions during the perioperative period may have the potential to improve clinical outcomes, enhance nutritional status, and positively impact quality of life in this patient population. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the effects of nutritional interventions during the perioperative phase for women with ovarian cancer. Comprehensive electronic searches were performed across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Gynaecological Cancer Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, Medline, Embase, DARE, AMED, BNI, and CINAHL, covering studies up to 2012. Additional searches included trials databases, conference proceedings, and citation lists, with no restrictions on language or publication date. Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) involving women aged 18 years or older with any stage of ovarian cancer, including recurrent disease, who were in the perioperative phase and received nutritional interventions, were eligible for inclusion. A total of 4092 titles were screened, and 14 full-text reports were reviewed. However, only one small RCT met the inclusion criteria. This study involved 40 women, 35 of whom had ovarian cancer, undergoing extensive elective surgery, including bowel resection, for the treatment of gynecological malignancies. Participants were randomised to either an early oral feeding group (oral fluids within the first 24 hours post-surgery, followed by solid foods the next day) or a traditional feeding regimen (oral intake delayed until bowel function was evident). In the early oral feeding group, the majority of women (14 out of 18) were able to resume eating solid food one day after surgery. This approach was associated with a significantly shorter hospital stay compared to the traditional feeding regimen, without an increase in postoperative complications or a negative impact on quality of life measures. The incidence of postoperative nausea and vomiting was similar between the two groups, affecting slightly more than half of the participants. Overall survival was assessed up to 30 days post-discharge, during which one death occurred in the traditional feeding group, though the cause of death was not reported. The risk of bias in the included study was assessed, and no high risk of bias was identified in its methodology or reporting. However, the small sample size and the fact that not all participants had ovarian cancer increased the risk of bias. The authors concluded that while women with ovarian cancer are at risk of malnutrition, there is a lack of robust evidence from RCTs addressing the identification, assessment, and treatment of malnutrition during the perioperative period. The findings from this small study suggest that early oral feeding (fluids within 24 hours and solids the following day) may be safe for some women undergoing surgery with bowel resection, without increasing complications. However, further research, including larger RCTs, is necessary to develop evidence-based guidelines for managing malnutrition in this patient population.
